quote: One good cue that you’re dealing with a “wrong question” is when you cannot even imagine any concrete, specific state of how-the-world-is that would answer the question.
content: The cue would have misfired at most of the great questions in the history of science before they were answered. In 1700 no one could imagine a concrete state of the world that would answer “what is heat?” or “what is the difference between a living and a dead body?”; the answers (molecular motion; a chemistry) were unimaginable in the required sense until the concepts that made them expressible had been built, and they were built by people trying to answer the question, not dissolve it. The cue is a version of the verificationist criterion of meaning that Book II’s annotations already found the essays disowning and reusing, and it was abandoned by its inventors because it could not be stated in a form that admitted universal laws and theoretical entities while excluding metaphysics (Hempel, “Problems and Changes in the Empiricist Criterion of Meaning,” Revue Internationale de Philosophie, 1950). The essay does not have a criterion that separates “no answer is imaginable because the question is confused” from “no answer is imaginable because the answer needs concepts we lack,” and it is the second that describes almost every question at the frontier. The book’s own commitments fail the cue: no concrete state of the world distinguishes “probability is in the mind” from its denial, or “reality is math” from “reality is described by math.”

quote: And no, I don’t know the answer to that last one. But I can guess one thing, based on my previous experience with unanswerable questions. The answer will not consist of some grand triumphant First Cause.
content: The “previous experience” consists of the tree-in-the-forest dispute and, on the essay’s own account, a free-will problem whose dissolution is assigned as homework and never shown. That is a sample of one, and the one is a definitional dispute that no one since Berkeley has thought was substantive. On the question actually named, “why does anything exist at all?,” the essay says no answer can even be imagined; the philosophical literature contains several, which is the difference between an unanswered question and a wrong one. Parfit’s “Why anything? Why this?” (London Review of Books, 1998) lays out the space of possible answers as a choice among “selectors” and asks which would be least arbitrary; van Inwagen, “Why Is There Anything at All?” (Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume, 1996) gives a probabilistic argument (there is one empty world among infinitely many possible ones, so the probability of nothing is zero); Nozick’s Philosophical Explanations (1981) has a chapter of candidates. One may think all of these fail. But each is a concrete answer-shaped thing, and their existence refutes the claim that none can be imagined. Predicting that the eventual resolution “will not consist of” any of them is a forecast with no track record behind it.

quote: Such questions must be dissolved. Bad things happen when you try to answer them. It inevitably generates the worst sort of Mysterious Answer to a Mysterious Question
content: “Inevitably” is not supported by anything in the essay, and the essay’s previous paragraph has already given a case where the opposite happened: the tree dispute, once someone asked what “sound” meant, was answered (two distinct claims, both true), and the answer is what dissolved it. The general pattern is that questions of the “what is X, really?” form are resolved by an answer that changes the question’s terms (heat, life, simultaneity), which is to say that answering and dissolving are not two different activities but one activity described before and after. The essay’s two categories, questions that are answered and questions that are dissolved, are separated only in hindsight: a question is called “wrong” once the answer has made it look confused, and called “answered” once the answer has made it look prescient. What the reader is told to do, in either case, is the same: find out how the phenomenon works. The essay’s contribution is a warning against the First Cause type of answer, which is a warning against a particular class of bad answers, not against answering.
